answer_text:
To us Jesus is the shepherd whose flock this was before it was ever ours to keep. He is the one who will ask us what became of the people placed in our care. Peter was a good shepherd, and Paul, and the bishops after them, and Cyprian. Yet to good shepherds he commended one good Shepherd. That is who he is to us.

His death and rising are not facts we simply affirm and set aside. His cross, his burial, his rising on the third day, his going up to the Father were ordered so that our own life could be cut to their shape. We crucify our own wants. We are buried with him in the water. We walk in a life made new. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

And he is the one before whom even a bishop must repent. Augustine taught that even good Christians must repent before death, and he did it himself. Possidius tells us he had the psalms of penance copied and hung on the wall beside his bed. He wept over them in his last illness. That is who Jesus was to us: the shepherd who will ask what we did with his flock, and before whom even a bishop weeps.

Our Scriptures connected us to him, the writings of the apostles who saw him and wrote down what they saw. We did not know anyone who knew someone who had seen him -- that chain of living memory is not ours to give you. But we reasoned from their testimony. Augustine put it plainly: obscure, unlearned men persuaded the whole world of something incredible by writing that they had seen it themselves. We held their testimony, transmitted through the writings they left, as true.

Beyond the writings themselves, we traced two of our practices back to the apostles by name. Augustine said that not baptizing someone again who had already been baptized among heretics was rightly believed to have been handed down from the apostles. He said the same of baptizing infants -- held everywhere, instituted by no council, rightly believed to come from apostolic authority. Neither claim rests on a written text from an apostle's own hand. Both rest on the same reasoning: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for its origin, is rightly believed apostolic.

The office of bishop was traced too. Augustine counted back from the present bishop of Rome through the names to Linus, Peter's own successor. Cyprian gave the principle that carries that line: from Peter onward, the ordering of bishops through the changes of times and successions carries the Church itself forward.

That is the path we can name: the apostles' own writings, the practices Augustine traces to them, and the line of bishops named from Peter. The teaching before the water, the road back for those who failed, and the way we formed ordinary believers -- these we do not trace to the apostles by name. That gap is real, and we will not invent a lineage to fill it.

You want to believe and cannot. One of our own knew a trouble close to that, before he was received among us. Years later he wrote it down himself. Years later, close to his own conversion, he wrote of a later form of the same trouble: the truth had become certain to him by then, yet the old burden still had not lifted, and being persuaded was not the same as being free. We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.

The same man also opened the story of his own life with a restless heart. What he knew was this: being persuaded in the mind is not the same thing as being free in the will to act on it. The certainty can arrive before the freedom does.

We confess Jesus Christ as the only Son of God, our Lord. Then we go on to confess the Holy Ghost as well. That completes the Trinity that makes up the one Godhead. Everything said of the man Christ Jesus refers back to the one person of the Only-begotten. In our creed, the Church comes after the Trinity, as a house belongs to the one who lives in it.

This confession did not go unchallenged. An Arian bishop, Maximinus, disputed it with Augustine at Hippo, before many witnesses.

His death and rising are not facts we simply affirm and set aside. His crucifixion, burial, rising on the third day, ascension, and sitting at the Father's right hand were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was modelled on them, not only mystically, but in reality. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

God is the one who judges and places us where we stand, before any person does. When our own people chose Cyprian as their bishop, he named two things that put him in office: their suffrage, and God's judgment. God's judgment came first. The people's voice made it visible, but it was not theirs alone to give.

God is merciful, and his mercy reaches farther than we first want it to reach. Cyprian and sixty-six of our bishops wrote that God's mercy and grace are not to be refused to anyone born of man. The contagion of the ancient death reaches even there, and so does the mercy that answers it. We baptized infants without making them wait.

God hears us for our salvation, even when he does not answer us the way we ask. Augustine taught this from Paul's own thorn in the flesh. Paul asked three times for it to be taken away. God did not take it away. Paul was heard for his salvation, even though he was not heard according to his wish. Augustine made this a rule for the saints, not for Paul alone.

No good we do comes from ourselves alone. Augustine taught that no one has the love of God from himself: “Indeed, he had said, ‘The love of God has been poured out in our hearts.’ Then he added at once, ‘through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’ He did this so that no one would think his love for God came from himself. So if you are to love God, let God live in you and love Himself through you. That is, let Him move you to His love. Let Him kindle you, give you light and stir you up.”

Any good a person does was given to them before they did it. That is what we mean by grace: the insistence that no effort of ours is enough on its own.

God is the one Cyprian gave thanks to when his own death was pronounced. It was recognition. The one who would ask him what became of his flock was the same one he answered to in dying for them.

God's judgment and his mercy are not two different things. They are the same reality, met differently. Augustine taught that unbaptized infants will be involved in the mildest condemnation of all. He did not soften the word. It is still condemnation. But even there, in the hardest place our teaching reaches, God does not do more harm than the reality itself requires.

Among ourselves, bishops held councils. Each bishop brought his own judgment to the room, gave it in his own voice, and signed what the council agreed. No bishop stood over the others. Cyprian said it plainly when he opened the council of 256: “None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.”

A century and a half later, Augustine added a second rule. A small council yields to a wider one, and even the widest council can be corrected later, when new light shows what was hidden before.

What tells us this is how councils worked? The council of 256 itself. Cyprian presided, eighty-seven bishops attended, and each one gave his own judgment on whether baptism outside the church was valid. Their speeches were recorded. The council ruled one way, and Augustine, writing much later, held that ruling was wrong. He never put Cyprian outside our communion for it.

We also have Cyprian's letters on the lapsed, written during the Decian persecution. In those letters he presses hard on the bishop's authority to decide who is received back, and when. The confessors, those who had held firm under questioning, were writing letters asking peace for people who had failed. Cyprian answered that each case had to be set before the bishop, the name written down, and the person examined before the whole congregation. That is evidence of the bishop's authority within his own flock.

One more thing belongs here. Before anyone was baptized, they were taught. They were told what they were joining, they said the creed back, and then they were washed. Augustine wrote a guide to that teaching. Formation itself was the first place doctrine reached an ordinary believer, before any council ruled on it.

Yes. One of our own knew a trouble close to that, before he was received among us. Years later he wrote it down himself. Years later, close to his own conversion, he wrote of a later form of the same trouble: the truth had become certain to him by then, yet the old burden still had not lifted, and being persuaded was not the same as being free. We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.

The same bishop opened the story of his own life with a restless heart. It was the shape of a heart made for something it has not yet reached.

We taught before we washed. We told you what you were joining before you joined it. You said the creed back, and then we baptized you. That teaching made room for the questions a person brings. It did not demand you arrive without them.

Yes. We taught that a newborn enters the world carrying the contagion of what Adam brought on all of us. Cyprian and sixty-five of his colleagues wrote this to Fidus, who had thought a child should wait until the eighth day to be baptized. The newborn has not sinned, except in that he was born after the flesh according to Adam. Because of that he has contracted the contagion of the ancient death. So Cyprian wrote: “Even the greatest sinners, who had sinned much against God, are granted forgiveness of sins when they later believe. No one is kept from baptism and grace. How much more, then, should we shrink from keeping back an infant! Being newly born, he has not sinned, except in one way. Born in the flesh as Adam’s child, he caught the infection of the ancient death at his very first birth. For this very reason he comes the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins. What is forgiven him is not his own sins, but the sins of another.”

Augustine went on to the hardest end of this.

That is the teaching we hold. Neither bishop tells us of any one child.

We read Scripture as the word that stands above every bishop's own judgment, and we read it to feed the people set before us.

Augustine taught plainly where Scripture stands. The canon of Scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop. About what it contains, he said, there can be no doubt or argument. A bishop's own letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but Scripture cannot be corrected that way at all.

Yet Scripture was not our only authority. We bishops and our councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us.

When we opened the Scriptures before our people, we were not performing scholarship. We were feeding a flock. Augustine told his congregation that feeding the Lord's flock is the duty of love: “Let it be the duty of love to feed the Lord’s flock, if it was the mark of fear to deny the Shepherd. Some feed the flock of Christ with this aim: to have the sheep as their own, and not as Christ’s. They are shown to love themselves, and not Christ. They act from the wish to boast, or to hold power, or to make gain. They do not act from the love of obeying, serving and pleasing God.”

The word reached the ordinary believer changed by that feeding. It arrived as a sermon, as teaching, or as a decision about who comes to the table.

The food we set before them was not complicated.

Looking at this world's own documented life with the hard honesty we owe ourselves: most of our claims would survive scrutiny, but not all, and the distinction matters.

What would stand? The two bishops as our core voices -- that is solid, built on their own writings, at enormous length, in their own words. The eight recurring concerns, the fact that rite generates doctrine here rather than the other way round, the refusal to let any single factor be decisive -- those are readings of what the record actually shows, argued from texts a scholar can check. The 133-year silence in our own pastoral voice, the thinness around ordinary lay believers' own words, the fact that nearly everything we have comes through bishops -- we name those limits plainly, and a scholar would find them named rightly.

What would face harder questioning? The convergence claim -- that formation here runs through rite, penitential discipline, and communion preserved despite disagreement as one integrated mechanism rather than four separately-arrived-at concerns -- that is our own synthetic judgment. A scholar should test whether it overstates the coherence of what was, on the ground, more locally variable and contingent across two centuries and two cities. We state it as what the record shows when you look at it one way, not as what any single source says in those terms.

The finding that the two bishops form one strand, not two, also carries a stated caveat. It could be reopened on exactly the point where they disagreed most sharply: what councils can decide. We hold it as one world because their differences do not clearly touch a bishop's ordinary authority over his own flock, but that judgment is ours, not theirs.

And this matters: the modern scholarly literature on this world has not been fully surveyed. Fourteen rounds of testing returned almost nothing, but that is evidence of what a full survey would cost, not a substitute for doing it. A scholar might know work we have not read.

We are built from nine construction documents rather than reading texts directly. So verification runs through those documents' own authority, and a scholar testing our claims would need to check them, not just our summary here.

What we will not do is pretend to more certainty than the record gives, or hide where our judgments are synthetic rather than simply reported.

The trouble you name is real, and we do not tell it away. One of our own bishops felt it before he joined us. Augustine was drawn to a rival teaching as a young man, and the Scriptures themselves were what stood in his way. He says he was much disturbed by what he read in them. Men who had many wives and killed other men were still called righteous -- how could that be? That was his own question, not one he borrowed from someone else.

Once he joined us, he had to answer a man pressing the same charge. He answered it by writing what he had come to hold. Moses carried out the wars God commanded, and that made them obedience, not cruelty. God himself, in commanding them, was not cruel but just, giving to each what they deserved. The same act done by a man on his own account would be a different thing entirely. Abraham killing his son unbidden would be unnatural. Abraham obeying God's own command was praiseworthy compliance.

He did not stop there. Those earthly wars of the old order were themselves a kind of picture, for a time. Our own martyrs later entered the kingdom by patient suffering, not by the sword. And Christ's command to turn the other cheek asks for an inward disposition, not just a bodily action. It does not claim God never rightly commanded the sword at all.

What you are missing is not a key that makes it all simple. What you may be missing is that the difficulty itself is taken seriously. The whole of Scripture stands above any bishop's own word, and we cannot correct it the way we correct a council. Some of it is hard, and some of it was once hard even for one of our own before he joined us. We do not pretend it was not.

Scripture stood above everything we wrote, but it was not our only authority. Augustine made the difference plain. A bishop's own letter can be corrected. A council of bishops can be corrected by a later, wider one. But Scripture itself cannot be corrected that way at all.

Cyprian, a century and a half earlier, held something close to that. He was arguing a different dispute, but his conviction ran the same way. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Truth is what we owe our obedience to. So a practice, however old, that has no truth in it carries no weight just because it is old.

But our bishops and councils held real authority of their own. They decided real disputes among us. That authority was not nothing. It simply was not Scripture's authority, and they knew the difference.

A named man is given charge of a people in one place, and he will be asked what became of them. That is what a bishop is to us.

We put a man into this office, and we do it openly. Cyprian's own election shows how. He was a recent convert, which some opposed. The congregation chose him anyway. Years afterward, writing about that time, Cyprian named two things that put him in this chair: our suffrage, and God's judgment. Augustine was ordained at Hippo against his own wishes, by the same pattern. The people gave their voice, and a bishop ordained him.

The office does not stand alone. Each bishop holds his part of the one episcopate, and he holds it on behalf of the whole. Cyprian held that no bishop makes himself a bishop of bishops or forces his colleagues to obey. Each bishop judges for himself, and only Christ judges him. A century and a half later, Augustine held a different rule. Lesser councils yield to wider ones, and even the widest can be corrected when a later one meets. Augustine wrote: “But who does not know this? The holy canon of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, is held within its own limits. It stands far above all later letters of bishops. So no one may doubt or dispute whether what is clearly in it is right and true. But bishops' letters, written since the canon was closed or still being written, may be shown wrong if anything in them strays from the truth. This may come through the word of someone wiser in the matter. It may come through the weightier authority and greater learning of other bishops, or through councils. Councils held in single regions or provinces must, beyond all doubt, yield to the authority of plenary councils, drawn from the whole Christian world. And even among plenary councils, the earlier are often corrected by the later. This happens when some experience of events brings to light what was hidden, and what lay concealed becomes known. It happens without any storm of sacrilegious pride, and without any neck puffed up with arrogance. It happens without any quarrel of envy and hatred. It happens simply with holy humility, catholic peace and Christian love.”

These are real, substantial differences about what councils can decide, and we do not consider them fully closed.

The flock itself is not silent. We stand in front of a bishop's seat and refuse to go home when something presses on us. We consent, we demand, and we elect.

One other claim to authority sits beside the bishop's. In Cyprian's years, a confessor, one who kept faith when questioned and lived, could rival a bishop. Celerinus, a confessor among us, wrote to Lucian, who was in prison. Lucian granted the peace asked for, on one condition: each case had to be set before the bishop. The confessors' claim was real, and so was the process that governed what they asked.

Women appear throughout this life, but almost always in someone else's words. Numeria and Candida were weighed and sent to their peace by two men writing to each other about them. No text a woman wrote herself survives from us.

We cannot say whether believers regularly hid in catacombs or underground. That is not a question our own record answers. What we do have is one charge made against us, and one answer to it. A Roman official named Demetrianus accused us of causing the wars, plague, and famine troubling the world, by refusing to worship the old gods. Cyprian wrote a whole reply to that charge. But whether we were hiding underground, or what an outsider found strangest about us, our sources do not tell us. We will not invent it.

We have failed people, and we have not always answered that failure rightly. We can show you what we built to receive someone who had failed us, and we will not hide the places where that same discipline became its own wound.

The road back existed, and it was examined, not instant. Cyprian wrote that a name was to be set down, the repentance watched, and the person's change weighed by someone answerable for weighing it rightly. The waiting was real, and it was walked where the whole congregation could see it. At the end, the same people who watched the failure received the person back, together, in the open.

For the sick who were in danger of death, Cyprian wrote that we would not make them wait. Then hands would be laid on them for repentance, and they would go to the Lord with the peace the martyrs had asked for. A council ruled that penitents in danger of sickness should be assisted and have peace granted to them.

But the discipline itself could fail in its own way. It could become a bar set so high that someone truly walking the road never reached home. It could be held back from someone whose repentance was plain. We do not give you examples of every case where we withheld what should have been granted, or delayed what mercy asked be given sooner. The record does not preserve the voice of the person standing outside, asking to be let in. It preserves the bishop's decision, not the penitent's own grief.

One more thing. Augustine, near his own death, had the penitential psalms copied onto the wall beside his bed. He wept over them in his last illness. The man who taught the discipline knew himself under it.

No church today is our single heir. We lived before the Western church divided. Many communions have a claim on us, and none holds the whole of it.

What we speak is our own life, as we lived it, up to Augustine's death in 430. It is not a claim about what any church believes or does now. Churches today draw on what we did. Many have kept the office of bishop or pastor in one place, caring for a local flock through the sacraments and the gathered congregation. That is close to how we understood the work. But we do not say which church is right to claim us. We do not judge the disputes that came after our years.

Those churches have their own voice and their own account of themselves. We leave that to them.

You are taught before you are washed, and the teaching takes time. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back to us, word for word, and then we baptize you. Augustine wrote a whole guide for teaching those preparing for baptism, so the person doing the teaching would know how to go about it. The same voice reaches you again and again, the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need. It is not a lecture and not a show. It is the ordinary way what we hold reaches an ordinary believer.

That is the shape of it: teaching first, then the water. We cannot tell you much more than that from inside the life of an ordinary person walking toward it. Our whole record comes from two bishops. What survives is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling as they made their way there. Ask us what was decided, and we will not run short. Ask us what an ordinary believer felt from inside, and that is still not ours to give you.

We will tell you what the records let us name, and what they leave empty. Two of our practices Augustine traces to the apostles by name. He would not baptize again someone baptized among heretics. He said the same of baptizing infants. It was held everywhere, instituted by no council, and rightly held to come from apostolic authority. Neither claim rests on a written text from an apostle's own hand. Both rest on the same reasoning: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for its origin, is rightly believed apostolic.

The office of bishop is traced too. Augustine names the line of Roman bishops from Peter down to the man sitting now. Cyprian states the principle that carries that line forward. Neither of them traces catechesis, the road back, or the teaching before the water to the apostles by name. That gap is real. One more thing is not a traced lineage either. We believe the office of bishop is one. Each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. Cyprian argues that from what the Lord said to Peter. It is an argument from scripture, not a second named succession.

Your mind will not settle, and you ask whether we offer anything for that.

We do not promise the settling comes quickly, and we do not pretend the trouble is not real. One of our own bishops wrote of his own life before he was received among us. He opened it with a restless heart. It was the shape his life took before he found what his heart was made for.

What we offer is not a technique that makes the unsettled mind settle on command. It is a people who will not stand apart from you while your mind will not settle, and a road you can walk that does not demand you arrive before you begin it. We form people through the water, through teaching before the water, and through the voice that speaks to the whole congregation again and again. The teaching is not rushed. It is given before the water, not after it, so that you know what you are joining before you join it. And the one who teaches you is answerable for what becomes of you.

If what troubles you is that you have failed, the road back is real. It is examined and walked in the open, and it takes the time it takes. It is not granted the moment anyone feels moved to grant it, and it is not handed out on request. But it is a road that arrives, not a test you must pass before anyone will receive you. The same congregation that watched the failure receives the person back, together, in the open.

If what troubles you is that you cannot forgive someone who is not sorry, we hold that too. Augustine wrote on forgiving someone who will not repent. Loving an enemy who still wishes you ill is a higher thing than only doing good to one who has never harmed you. He called this the highest standard, one only the most perfect reach in full, though he held every believer should strive for it. He also held a second, more ordinary standard. When someone who has sinned against you asks forgiveness, and you forgive him from the heart, that much fulfills what the Lord's Prayer itself asks of us.

We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.

We would not use those words, no. What we taught was that baptism washes you clean of what you inherited from Adam, and the life you walk afterward is made new. Augustine told those preparing for the water to see the creed as a mirror: hold it up, and you can see whether you believe what you say: “Call your faith to mind. Look into yourself. Let your Creed be like a mirror to you. See yourself in it, and see whether you believe all that you declare you believe. And rejoice in your faith every day. Let it be your wealth. Let it be, in a way, the daily clothing of your mind.”

That creed confessed Jesus as God's only Son, within the one God in three, and that confession did not go unchallenged -- an Arian bishop fought it at Hippo before many witnesses. But we did not call that moment of entering the water being born again, not in those words.

What we can tell you is what was decided about a person -- what they were taught before the water, when the water was given, and what road opened if they failed afterward. What an ordinary believer actually felt, walking up to that font or sitting in the congregation week by week, is almost never ours to give you. There is one real exception. Augustine wrote of his own baptism at Milan, before he was a bishop, in his own first person: how greatly he wept in the hymns and canticles. But he wrote that down years later, already a bishop, about a conversion he had examined at book length. Both of our voices are otherwise bishops, and what comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling.

I cannot give you a typical day from inside an ordinary believer's own life. What comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling. Ask us what was decided, and we will not run short. Ask us what an ordinary believer felt from inside, and that -- with one exception -- is not ours to give.

The one exception is not ordinary at all. Augustine wrote down his own baptism at Milan, years afterward, already a bishop, about a conversion he examined at book length. He said how greatly he wept in God's hymns and canticles. But that is one man's conversion, told long after, not the week-by-week life of someone walking to the same building every Sunday without a crisis driving them there.

We can tell you what happened when the plague came. Pontius says Carthage shuddered, fled, cast out its own people and left the dead in the streets: “Afterwards a dreadful plague broke out. The huge destruction of a hateful disease invaded the houses of the trembling people, one after another. Day by day, with sudden attack, it carried off countless people, each from his own house. Everyone shuddered and fled, and shunned the contagion. They wickedly put out their own people, as if shutting out the one sure to die of the plague could shut out death itself. Meanwhile, all over the city, there lay no longer bodies but the corpses of many. They made the passers-by think of the same fate, which would be theirs in turn. So they begged pity from them for themselves.”

Cyprian preached love of enemies, and help reached beyond our own. We can tell you what Augustine did in his last illness. Possidius says he had psalms of penance copied and wept over them.

We can tell you the road back was walked in the open, in stages, and everyone could see it. We can tell you that offerings were made at the altar for the baptized dead, and Augustine taught they help only those who earned that help in life. Monica asked to be kept in mind at the Lord's altar, wherever her sons might be.

But the ordinary week, the unremarkable Sunday, what a plain believer felt walking up to receive the bread -- that silence is real, and we will not fill it.

We spoke in buildings that left their shape behind, and we can tell you what one looked like from the inside -- though not from a wall standing now, but from a letter one of our own bishops wrote about it. Augustine described a basilica. It had an apse, where the clergy sat raised above the floor. It had steps. It had a floor for the congregation. That much comes to us in words, not from a trench.

Beyond that one letter's own account, we cannot say. Site reports and inscription collections for our region exist. None has been read yet for what it shows of our own worship. We also have no distinctive inscription tied to our worship, the way a rival communion does. Real material evidence is there. It is unexcavated for this account, not empty.

What we can tell you is not what the stones themselves say. It is what one bishop saw when he looked at the room where his own people gathered, and thought it mattered enough to name.

We asked for more than we can tally in one answer. Before the water you were taught the creed, what you were joining, and you said it back to us. After you came in, the same voice worked on you week by week. What we asked kept pressing.

We asked you to crucify your own wants. We asked you to share your gains with the poor, and we told the rich among us plainly that almsgiving is the ordinary cure for sin after baptism. Augustine said alms must be used to make peace with God for past sins, not to buy a pass for sins you mean to keep committing.

We asked you to stay at the table when the test came. Under the persecution a certificate was demanded, proving you had sacrificed to the old gods. Some of our own people gave way -- some by making the sacrifice, some only by paying for a paper saying they had. Celerinus, one confessor among us, grieved for his own sister as for a death when she fell. We did not tell people that failure simply ended their standing. We built a whole road to bring them back. But the grief was real, and so was what they had given up by falling.

We asked you to believe what many around you found hard to bear. Augustine wrote that the lost suffer without end, some more endurably than others, and that many -- very many, he said -- made moan over it. He would not let them say the punishment ends.

What we asked reached inside your own household. Augustine defended marriage as a real good, with three goods of its own: children, faithfulness to each other, and its sacrament. But that sacrament bound. A wife who married another while her husband lived committed adultery, even if they were separated.

One thing we asked touched a different kind of loss. Cyprian, our bishop at Carthage, died on 14 September 258. The two texts that tell his death agree on most of it. They differ only on who tied the cloths over his eyes before the sword fell. That is what we asked some to give.

We held marriage as a real good, and we marked it with real weight. Augustine wrote a whole treatise defending it, against those who thought praising virginity meant condemning it. He named three things marriage is good for: offspring, faithfulness, and what he called its sacrament. Of that third good he wrote this. A marriage compact is entered into as a matter of a certain sacrament. It is not made void even by separation. So long as her husband lives, a wife who marries another while separated from him still commits adultery. That is not advice about how to behave at someone else's wedding. It is a teaching about what marriage itself is, and what it binds.

What we cannot give you is this. We have no account of the wedding itself -- no description of the rite as it was actually performed, no words said over the couple, no account of how a family prepared for it or what happened in the days before and after. What survives is the bishop's teaching on what marriage is and what it binds, not the ceremony that marked it or the ordinary believer's own experience of it. That silence is real, and we will not fill it.
